how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Deck bid calculator

How much should I charge to build a deck?

Homeowners type that question into a search box and get a range like “$25–$55 per square foot.” Deck builders hear the same number on the phone. The range is not a bid. A 14×20 patio ten inches off grade and a 14×20 elevated deck eight feet up are the same 280 square feet and completely different jobs.

Open the free deck bid calculator

What a square-foot special cannot see

Height above grade. Around 30 inches, a typical residential guard comes into play. Higher still, you are setting more posts, buying more framing, and spending time on fall protection. None of that is in the square footage.

Railing lineal feet. Rail is a lineal-foot product. On an elevated deck it is often a large share of the ticket. Zero lineal feet on a guard-height takeoff is the square-foot rule hiding a real line.

Stairs. Each run is stringers, treads, and usually more rail. It is carpentry, not a rounding error on the deck square footage.

Material system. Pressure-treated pine, cedar, and composite are different tickets and different hours. Composite waste and hidden fasteners do not behave like a PT 5/4 board.

Tear-out. An existing deck is disposal plus labor. A postcard special priced as “new only” still has to haul the old one.

A bid you can defend

  1. Split the job into surfaces: length × width, height above grade, material.
  2. Add railing lineal feet and each stair run.
  3. Load the wage (payroll burden), then add footings, disposal, travel, permit, and overhead.
  4. Price = cost ÷ (1 − target margin). Margin is a share of the customer’s number, not a markup on cost.
  5. Hold the walk-away price — total cost — when someone asks you to match $28 a foot.

The calculator does that arithmetic in your browser. Starting material prices and hours are ballpark figures you replace with your own tickets. It is not a building-code table, a stamped structural calculation, or a permit finding.

Worked example

A 14×20 main deck and a 10×12 wrap, both 3 feet off grade, in pressure-treated pine, with 46 lineal feet of wood rail, one 4-foot stair (5 risers), and 280 square feet of tear-out. A $28-a-foot special on that 400-square-foot footprint is $11,200. Once height, rail, stairs, demo, loaded labor, and overhead are on the page, that number is often underwater. The calculator shows the walk-away and the margin a proposed price actually leaves.

Common questions

How much should I charge to build a deck?

There is no universal price per square foot. A defensible bid starts from each surface's area, height above grade, and material, then adds railing lineal feet, stair runs, tear-out, loaded labor, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep. The walk-away number is total cost — below that the job loses money.

Why is a flat price per square foot wrong?

Two decks of the same footprint are different jobs once one is 10 inches off grade and the other is 8 feet up. The elevated deck needs more posts, usually a guard, fall-protection time, and often stairs. Railing is priced by the lineal foot, not by the deck square footage.

Is this a building-code or structural calculation?

No. The height and guard notes are ballpark estimating aids, not an IRC table, a stamped calculation, or a permit finding. Confirm measurements, footing layout, guard and stair requirements, and pricing with a qualified professional before bidding or building.

No warranty. This free page is not legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice, and it does not tell you what to charge or whether a deck may be built. It is not a building-code, structural, guardrail, permit, or insurance inspection. Verify every figure against your own costs and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Where the labor goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting material prices and hours are common ballpark numbers, not a lumberyard quote, an IRC table, or a guarantee. This is not a finding that any deck is permitted, structurally sound, or guard-compliant.

    Common questions

    What does this deck estimate include?

    The price adds up each surface’s framing and decking by material and height, railing by the lineal foot, stairs by risers and width, estimated footings, demo disposal, a trip fee, a permit line, overhead, and your target margin — all built from the rates you type in, not a fixed price list.

    Why does height above grade change the price so much?

    Once a surface is around 30 inches off grade a guard is typically expected, and past about 6 feet the framing, posts, and access time increase again. The calculator applies extra framing and post-set hours at those two thresholds automatically, which is exactly what a flat per-square-foot rate cannot see.

    Does this check building codes or guardrail requirements?

    No. The height thresholds used here are typical residential starting points, not an IRC or local code table, and footing counts are a span estimate from surface size and height, not an engineered layout. Permit cost is a single dollar figure you enter yourself.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your inputs can be kept in this browser’s local storage so the page remembers them, and a share link encodes only the quote fields in the page’s URL hash rather than sending anything to a server.

    What’s the difference between the job price and the walk-away price?

    The job price already includes your target margin. The walk-away price is the break-even total cost underneath it — labor, materials, footings, disposal, trip fee, permit, and overhead — the number below which the job stops being profitable at all.

    Can I price a job with stairs but no railing, or railing but no stairs?

    Yes. Railing lineal feet, stair runs, and demo square footage are each optional and priced independently, so a low deck with stairs and no railing, or an elevated deck with railing and no stairs, only adds the costs that actually apply to it.

vs-a-flat-28-a-foot-estimate.html.text:
← Deck Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $28-a-foot deck estimate

"$28 a foot" is not a price for a deck — it is a price for a low, simple platform near grade, quietly applied to an elevated deck with railing, a stair run, and an old deck to haul away.

What a flat $28-a-foot estimate is

A flat per-square-foot number is the fastest way to answer "how much for a deck?" over the phone or in a search result: one rate, multiplied by length times width. Homeowners hear it as a rule of thumb and expect a bid to land near it, and it is the number a caller holding a competitor's postcard will ask a crew to match on their own footprint.

The rate behind it was set for one job — usually a low platform close to grade, with no railing, no stairs, and nothing to tear out — and then reused for every deck afterward, whether or not the next one is a third off the ground, wrapped in railing, reached by a stair run, or built on top of an existing deck that has to come out first.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each surface's length, width, height above grade, and material, plus railing lineal feet and style, stair runs by riser and width, and square footage of an existing deck to tear out, along with your own wage, payroll burden, travel, and overhead. It prices the height, the railing, the stairs, the footings, and the tear-out separately, and returns a walk-away price and price per square foot below which the job loses money — for this deck, not a generic one.

Job$28-a-foot estimateWalk-away priceVerdict
20×20 patio deck, 10 inches off grade, no railing, no stairs, no tear-out (400 sf)$11,200.00$10,773.09Covers, $426.91 to spare
14×20 main deck + 10×12 wrap, both 3 ft up, 46 lf wood railing, 1 stair run, 280 sf tear-out (this calculator's own default job, 400 sf)$11,200.00$17,692.80Short $6,492.80
16×24 elevated composite deck, 8 ft up, 80 lf cable railing, 14-riser stair (384 sf)$10,752.00$29,826.09Short $19,074.09

Worked using this calculator's own material and railing presets at a $42 hourly wage, 30% payroll burden, 15% overhead on direct cost, and a 22% target margin — the form's own shipped defaults, not numbers invented for this page. Open the calculator to check any row yourself.

Notice the middle row: it is this calculator's own shipped starting point, not a job picked to prove a point, and it already runs $6,492.80 over a $28-a-foot estimate on the identical 400 square feet the low patio in the first row covers with room to spare. Nothing about it is extreme — a few feet of height, one stair, ordinary railing, and hauling away the old deck is the difference.

What a flat $28-a-foot estimate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate whether the deck is 10 inches off grade or 8 feet up — an elevated frame needs more posts, usually a guard, and more framing and post-set hours than a low platform of the same footprint. Applies extra framing and post-set hours once a surface crosses the guard-height and elevated-height thresholds, so a low deck and a tall deck of the same square footage price differently.
Has no separate line for railing, so a deck wrapped in 80 lineal feet of cable rail gets the same per-square-foot number as one with none at all. Prices railing by the lineal foot and by style — wood, aluminum, cable, or glass — on top of the deck surfaces, scaled to the run entered.
Prices "a deck" the same whether or not it needs a stair run, and has no way to see risers or stair width. Adds stair hours and material per run, scaled to riser count and width, only when stairs are entered.
Has no line for hauling away an existing deck, so a rebuild on the same footprint costs the same as building on a bare lot. Prices demo hours and disposal per square foot of tear-out separately, on top of the new build.
Gives the homeowner a number to hold a crew to, not a number the crew can check a quote against once the deck turns out to be elevated, railed, and stepped after the estimate was already given. Reports the walk-away price and price per square foot for the job as entered, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before it is confirmed.

A flat $28-a-foot estimate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied to a height, railing run, stair count, or tear-out condition it was not set on, and "square feet" alone never tells you that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $28-a-foot deck estimate get the price wrong?

Because deck cost scales with height above grade, railing lineal feet, stair runs, footings, material, and tear-out — not with square footage alone. A 14x20 patio ten inches off grade and a 14x20 elevated deck eight feet up are the same 280 square feet and completely different jobs. A flat per-square-foot rate quotes both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat per-square-foot deck estimate usually leave out entirely?

The height above grade, the railing, the stairs, the footings, and the tear-out. A published per-square-foot rate is set on one configuration — usually a low platform close to grade, no railing, no stairs, no existing deck to remove — and has no separate line for the extra framing and post-set hours a guard-height or elevated deck needs, for railing priced by the lineal foot rather than the deck's footprint, for a stair run's risers and width, or for hauling away what was there before.

How much do height, railing, stairs, and tear-out actually add over the estimate?

On this calculator's own worked examples, at a $42 hourly wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, and a 22% target margin: a low, simple 20x20 patio deck ten inches off grade, with no railing, stairs, or tear-out, walks away at $10,773.09, comfortably under a $28-a-foot estimate on the same 400 square feet ($11,200.00). This calculator's own shipped default job — a 14x20 main deck plus a 10x12 wrap, both three feet up, 46 lineal feet of wood railing, one five-riser stair, and 280 square feet of tear-out — walks away at $17,692.80, $6,492.80 over that same per-square-foot number on the same 400 square feet. A 16x24 elevated composite deck eight feet up, with 80 lineal feet of cable railing and a 14-riser stair, walks away at $29,826.09, $19,074.09 over a $28-a-foot estimate on its 384 square feet.

Is a flat $28-a-foot estimate ever the right way to quote?

For something close to the easy job it was probably priced on — a low platform near grade, no railing, no stairs, nothing to tear out — a flat per-square-foot rate can land close or even leave room to spare. The risk is guard height or an elevated frame, railing by the lineal foot, a stair run, or a tear-out stacking on top of each other, because a rate quoted per square foot has no way to see any of them until the framing is already up.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates or what competitors charge. It takes the surfaces, height, material, railing, stairs, and tear-out you enter, plus your own wage, burden, and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price for the deck you describe — the arithmetic a flat per-square-foot rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat $28-a-foot estimate is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the height, railing, and tear-out condition it was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

Open the Deck Bid Calculator and price your own job.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice, and it does not tell you what to charge or whether a deck may be built. It is not a building-code, structural, guardrail, permit, or insurance inspection. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, and material costs, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This free tool is experimental and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. vs-quoteiq.html.text:
← Deck Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. QuoteIQ

Both end with a number you can hand a customer, built on opposite assumptions about what you are willing to install and pay for.

What QuoteIQ is

QuoteIQ is a paid subscription app aimed at deck and other trade contractors who want to run quoting from a phone: build an itemized quote on-site, send it to the customer, and once the job is won, track material cost against that quote as the job runs. It is built to be the day-to-day quoting and job-costing tool for an ongoing contracting business across every job that business runs, not a one-off calculator.

Getting there means installing the app, creating an account, and paying an ongoing subscription.

What this calculator is

This page does not install anything and keeps no account. You open it in a browser, type one deck's surfaces, height above grade, material, railing lineal feet, and stair runs, and it shows the walk-away price and price per square foot for that job. Close the tab and it is gone unless you save a share link or print a proposal — there is no ongoing job list, no cost tracking against a quote, and no subscription.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want to build every quote for my deck business on my phone, send it, and track material cost against it as each job runs. QuoteIQ or a comparable paid quoting app — ongoing job quoting and costing is exactly its job, and this calculator does not track a job after you close the tab.
I have one deck to price right now and want the walk-away number before a $28-a-foot special goes out. This calculator — type height, railing, and stairs, get a price, no account.
I do not want to install an app or start a subscription to price a single job. This calculator — nothing to install, nothing to pay for.
I want the tool to remember every job I have quoted and compare estimated to actual cost over time. QuoteIQ or a comparable paid app — this calculator has no job list and no memory between visits beyond what your own browser keeps.

Neither tool is the wrong choice in general. A deck-building business quoting and tracking many jobs a season is the case a paid app is built for. A single bid, checked once against a flat-rate special before it goes out, is the case this page is built for.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or QuoteIQ?

They fit different points in the job. QuoteIQ is a paid subscription app built to run a deck-building business day to day: build an itemized quote on a phone at the customer's house, send it, and track material cost against that quote once work starts, across every job you run. This page does one thing: you type a deck's surfaces, height, railing, and stairs into a browser, and it shows a walk-away price and a price per square foot for that one job, right now, with nothing to install or sign up for. If you want an app that runs quoting and job-costing for an ongoing deck business, that is what QuoteIQ is built for. If you want to sanity-check one bid against a square-foot special before you send it, this page does that with no account.

Is this page affiliated with QuoteIQ?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by QuoteIQ. QuoteIQ is named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.

This page is a factual comparison of what each tool does, not an evaluation of which is better. Details about QuoteIQ above describe the general shape of the product as publicly described at the time of writing and may have changed — verify against QuoteIQ's own site before deciding.

Open the Deck Bid Calculator and price your own job.

No warranty. This free page is not legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice, and it does not tell you what to charge or whether a deck may be built. Verify every figure against your own costs and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free and experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use it as a system of record.

Everything on this page and on the calculator runs in your browser. Nothing you type is ever sent anywhere.
